sentences.text: This animal is classified as a long-snouted dyrosaurid.
It shared its environment with Titanoboa, the largest known snake, which weighed 1.2 tons.
The genus was described in 2011 by Alexander K. Hastings, Jonathan Bloch, and Carlos A. Jaramillo from fossils found in the Cerrejón coal mine in northeastern Colombia.
The name honors the river Acheron, a branch of the river Styx in Greek mythology meaning 'river of woe', referencing its habitat in a large river emptying into the Caribbean Sea.
Its slender ischial shaft suggests that the muscles controlling its position in water were less developed than in oceanic relatives.
A thin ischial axis indicates that the muscles controlling its position in the water were less developed.
It most likely fed on lungfishes and eels in inland rivers.
Acherontisuchus primarily ate fish, aided by its long, narrow snout which was similar to that of modern false gharials.
In these inland rivers, Acherontisuchus likely fed on dipnoan fish and eels.
Hastings suggested that while juvenile Acherontisuchus likely faced risks from Titanoboa, adults might have been too large for the 13-meter snake to prey upon.
Phylogenetic analysis places it in a derived clade of dyrosaurids alongside Hyposaurus, Congosaurus, Atlantosuchus, Rhabdognathus, and Guarinisuchus.
Acherontisuchus belongs to the subfamily Hyposaurinae.
Acherontisuchus is classified within the family Dyrosauridae.
The type species of the genus Acherontisuchus is Acherontisuchus guajiraensis.
Acherontisuchus is a member of the class Reptilia.
Acherontisuchus is closely related to other dyrosaurids found in both Africa and America.
It lived in Middle to Late Paleocene deposits of Colombia.
It lived in South America during the Paleocene, approximately 60 million years ago.
It lived in calm, shallow, inland freshwater habitats within the tropical rainforests of northeastern Colombia.
Acherontisuchus lived between 61.66 and 56 million years ago during the Selandian to Thanetian stages.
Acherontisuchus lived in a freshwater and tropical rainforest habitat in northern Colombia.
Because relationships among dyrosaurids are not well resolved, Acherontisuchus was placed in a polytomy with Hyposaurus, Congosaurus, and a group containing other close relatives.
